tip: Apa kabar? is literally 'what news?' – the everyday 'how are you?'. The stock reply: Kabar baik (good news = I'm fine).
Indonesian verbs never change for past tense – sudah does the work: Saya sudah makan siang = I already ate lunch. It's a completion marker, not a verb form.
belum means 'not yet' and implies it will still happen: Saya belum sarapan = I haven't had breakfast yet. Even 'are you married?' is answered with belum, not tidak.
akan puts a sentence in the future without touching the verb: Saya akan pergi = I will go. pergi keeps the same form in past, present, and future.
silakan invites someone to do something for their own benefit: Silakan duduk = please have a seat. tolong is the other 'please' – it asks someone to help you.
Commands are negated with jangan, not tidak: jangan pergi = don't go. tidak only states facts (dia tidak pergi = he doesn't go) – it can't forbid anything.
Boleh saya pinjam? asks permission (may I). bisa is ability (can): saya bisa berenang = I can swim. English 'can' covers both jobs; Indonesian splits them.
mari kita + verb = 'let's': mari kita mulai = let's begin. mari is the polite version – among friends you'll hear ayo instead: Ayo mulai!
tutup never changes for tense – sudah alone tells you the shop 'was already closed': sudah tutup. Time in Indonesian lives in the markers, not in verb endings.
Duration 'for' is selama, not untuk: mati selama dua jam = out for two hours. untuk is 'for' as purpose or recipient (untuk kamu = for you).
You drink medicine in Indonesian, even pills: minum obat is literally 'drink medicine'. There's no separate 'take' verb for it.
capek is the everyday spoken 'tired': Badan saya capek. The formal counterpart is lelah – same meaning, but capek is what you'll actually hear in conversation.
bilang is the conversational 'say': Dokter bilang saya harus istirahat = the doctor said. Formal writing prefers berkata or mengatakan – bilang is for speech.
tidak apa-apa is literally 'not anything' – doubling apa (what) turns it into 'anything', so the whole phrase means 'it's nothing, no problem'.
paling = 'the most' and never changes the word after it: paling kamu suka = you like the most. English swaps to -est or 'most'; Indonesian just drops in paling.
Order decides the meaning: jam tujuh = seven o'clock, but tujuh jam = seven hours. jam first reads the clock; the number first counts a duration.
susah + a di- verb = 'hard to get X-ed': susah ditelepon = hard to reach, literally 'hard to be phoned'. Same pattern with other verbs: susah dicari = hard to find.
Boleh saya lihat kamarnya? asks permission – and boleh alone is also the answer: Boleh! = sure, go ahead. One word for both the asking and the granting.
Bisa minta peta? is the complete everyday request – no subject, no 'give me' verb. minta = ask for a thing; bisa softens it into 'can I get...?'
jangan lupa = don't forget, the go-to reminder opener: jangan lupa bawa paspor. jangan negates commands; tidak lupa would just describe someone who doesn't forget.
The me- prefix turns a root into an active verb: inap (stay over) becomes menginap = to stay overnight. Kami menginap di hotel = we stayed at a hotel.
paling lambat is literally 'slowest' – Indonesian deadlines are superlatives: paling lambat hari Jumat = by Friday at the latest.
akan marks the future, but a time word can carry it alone: with besok in the sentence, kami akan rapat could drop the akan. It just makes 'will' explicit.
mati means dead or off, so matikan lampu is literally 'deaden the lamp' – the -kan ending turns the state into something you do to an object.
diadakan comes from ada (exist) – literally 'made to exist', the standard way to say an event 'is held': diadakan di rumah nenek = held at grandma's house.
One root, two people: pelajar learns, pengajar teaches – both from ajar. The pe- prefix builds 'the person who does X' nouns.
jam lima = five o'clock, but flip it and lima jam = five hours. Dad leaves at jam lima – word order alone separates clock time from duration.
ke-...-an can mark something that happened by accident: dompetku ketinggalan = my wallet got left behind, no one did it on purpose. Also kehujanan = got rained on.
masih = still ongoing: masih buka = still open. tetap also translates 'still' but means 'anyway, regardless' – tetap buka = stays open no matter what.
-nya glued to the end of a verb means 'it': menghabiskannya = finished it. The object attaches straight onto the verb – no separate word for 'it' needed.
Dia bilang dia akan datang – bilang connects straight to what was said, no word for 'that' required. Indonesian happily skips the connector English leans on.
belum tentu is literally 'not yet certain' – the Indonesian 'not necessarily': kabar itu belum tentu benar = that news isn't necessarily true.
dulu has two jobs: after sejak it means long ago (sejak dulu = since way back), but after a verb it means 'first' (makan dulu = eat first). Position decides.
Menurut saya is literally 'according to me' – menurut means 'following'. Indonesian frames opinions like citing a source, even when the source is you.
pernah packs 'have ever, at least once' into one word: kita pernah bertemu = we have met before. The negative is belum pernah = never (so far).
saya pikir X, ternyata Y is the stock reversal frame: saya pikir ini mudah, ternyata sulit = I thought it was easy – turns out it's hard. ternyata = it turns out.
The -kan ending changes what tanya points at: plain tanya takes the person you ask, menanyakan takes the topic – menanyakan harga = ask about the price.
sempat = had a spare moment and used it: sempat tanya kabar = found a moment to ask after your family. No single English word covers it.
biaya kirim = shipping cost, but shops and apps nearly always shorten it to ongkir (from ongkos kirim). Gratis ongkir = free shipping – you'll see it everywhere.
Struknya mau dibawa? is the stock checkout question – cashiers ask it at nearly every register. struk = receipt; answer Mau (yes please) or Tidak usah (no need).
maju means go forward, and on a schedule forward = earlier: rapat maju jadi jam delapan = the meeting moved up to eight. The opposite, postponed, is diundur.
paling lambat besok siang = by tomorrow noon at the latest. Its partner is paling cepat (at the earliest) – the pair brackets any deadline window.
tinggal usually means live or stay, but here it means 'remaining': waktu kita tinggal dua hari = we only have two days left. Context decides which tinggal you've met.
jauh-jauh hari is literally 'far-far days' – doubling jauh stretches the distance in time, giving 'well in advance': ajukan jauh-jauh hari.
masuk literally means enter, but by itself it means coming in to work or school: saya tidak bisa masuk = I can't come in. tidak masuk is the standard 'absent'.
